newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australis in tie-up talks with Optus.
newsitem.headline: Australis in tie-up talks with Optus.

text.p: Pay-tv operator Australis Media Ltd said on Wednesday it was in talks aimed at industry rationalisation with fellow pay tv operator Optus Vision.
"Talks are taking place with Optus and we expect a rationalisation of the industry to take place in the next three months," an Australis spokesman told Reuters.
Australis could not say if the talks were over a merger or not, he said. But he said Australis wanted to be part of the industry rationalisation that all players agreed was needed.
Optus Vision could not comment on whether or not it was in talks with Australis, an Optus Vision spokeswoman said.
Industry sources said Australis, which operates the Galaxy satellite and microwave television services, was in direct merger talks with Optus Vision and was also talking to Foxtel.
Foxtel is a joint venture between News Corp Ltd and the government-owned telecommunications group Telstra Corp.

Optus Vision is being merged with major shareholder Optus Communications. Major shareholders in the merged group include Mayne Nickless Ltd, US West Inc, the Seven Network and Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd.
"All three operators recognise there needs to be a fairly radical restructuring of industry, which is losing heavily," one well placed source said.

The three operators have lost about A$1.5 billion on pay television in the last three years as they poured money into the infrastrucuture of laying cables and setting up programming deals and local programmes.
Australis itself lost A$141.93 million in the first half of its current year to June 30, 1997, while Foxtel lost A$98 million in its first half.
Telstra was reported earlier this week to be in talks with News to shorten its cable rollout to about two million homes from initial plans for four million because of the high costs.

Industry sources said anti-monopoly concerns continue to be the major hurdle facing any mergers, but that the impending de-regulation of the telecommunications sector on July 1 may alleviate some of these concerns.
The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission has already rejected one attempt by Australis and Foxtel to merge.
Another hurdle seen to a potential Australis-Optus merger is the A$4.5 billion deal Australis has to supply programming to Foxtel over 25 years.
One solution, sources said, would be to somehow quarantine the revenue stream from the programming deal into a joint venture vehicle at arms length from the merged Australis/Optus unit.
Floats worth up to A$12 billion planned before the end of 1997 by Telstra and Optus are seen the driving factors in the push for rationalisation of the pay television industry.
Investors are seen reluctant to commit such large sums until they are sure the pay television sector they would be exposed to has stopped haemorrhaging such large losses.
The three operators currently have about 580,000 subscribers between them with Australis' Galaxy on 100,000, Australis' franchisees about 125,000, Foxtel with 175,000 and Optus about 180,000.
